newsitem.title: USA: Jones case could damage Clinton presidency.
newsitem.headline: Jones case could damage Clinton presidency.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

A U.S. Supreme Court decision to allow Paul Jones' sexual harassment case against President Bill Clinton to proceed could be enormously damaging to the president's political agenda, analysts said on Tuesday.

"At best from Clinton's viewpoint, it trivialises the presidency. At worst, it will deflect enormous attention from his political agenda," said Robert Holsworth, a political scientist at Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond.
"Clinton seemed to have successfully remade his image, only now to be dragged back into the muck," he said.
The court ruled 9-0 on Tuesday that the U.S. Constitution does not require that the politically embarrassing lawsuit be delayed until Clinton leaves office in 2001.

Jones, a former Arkansas state employee, alleged that then-Governor Clinton made unwanted sexual advances to her in a Little Rock hotel in 1991, including exposing himself to her and asking her to perform oral sex.

The prospect of the case now coming to trial would be a public relations nightmare for Clinton and his political advisers. But it may be difficult to settle out of court. Negotiations last year for a settlement ended in failure and Jones has little incentive now to agree to a deal.
"If I were the president's lawyer, I would advise him to settle this almost at any cost," said Jamin Raskin, a legal scholar at the American University in Washington.

He noted the furore surrounding other recent sexual cases, such as the adultery case of Air Force pilot Kelly Flinn, assault charges against NBC sports commentator Marv Albert and the rape trial of a member of the Kennedy family in 1991.
"The nation is almost obsessed by sexual cases but this would be so huge it would make all previous cases seem trivial," said Raskin.

The judgment comes at a time when Clinton is riding high in public opinion polls. With the economy still booming, he was able to use his increased prestige to achieve a landmark balanced budget deal with Republicans.

This setback may now remove some of his political leverage and embolden his enemies. The fact that the justices were unanimous makes it impossible for Clinton to argue that conservatives on the Supreme Court were out to get him.

"Clinton seems very presidential right now, before this bombshell. The big question is, will he now be cut down to the size he was in the first two years of his presidency?" said Steven Wayne, a political scientist at Georgetown University.
Opinion polls show many Americans have a poor opinion of Clinton's personal morals, but most have set those misgivings aside because of his success in managing the economy.
Dealing with a weakened Clinton may encourage Republicans to revert to a more confrontational style of politics.

It could also embolden Democratic rivals such as House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt, who is anxious to promote his own ambitions for the presidential election in 2000 at the expense of Clinton and his heir-apparent, Vice President Al Gore.
"Anything that damages Clinton indirectly damages Gore," said Holsworth. "He has more to lose than almost anybody."

Additionally, this decision is only the first of many legal trip wires awaiting Clinton. The Supreme Court must also rule this summer on the White House's argument that notes relating to testimony given by first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton on the Whitewater land scandal are privileged.
Raskin said he regarded the White House case on that issue to be much weaker than its argument in the Paula Jones case.

Whitewater special prosecutor Kenneth Starr must soon make the crucial decision of whether to indict Hillary Rodham Clinton. One of Starr's aides confirmed this was under discussion in an audio tape obtained by a reporter.
"This decision could encourage Starr," said Holsworth.
Republicans investigating alleged campaign fund raising misdeeds by the Clinton re-election campaign and the Democratic Party may also redouble their efforts.

The decision also puts womens groups, who have been among Clinton's most faithful supporters, in a bind. Feminists have been largely silent about Jones' claim of sexual harassment, a silence they may find it hard to maintain.
